sections.heading: Which Tickets Go to El Paso Municipal Court
paragraphs: El Paso Municipal Court is the busiest traffic court in the region because it belongs to the City of El Paso, and the city's police department writes more citations than every other agency in the county combined. If an EPPD officer stopped you — on I-10, Mesa St, Montana Ave, Loop 375, Zaragoza Rd, Dyer St or any neighborhood street inside the city limits — your ticket is filed downtown at 810 E. Overland Ave. That includes speeding, red light and stop sign violations, no insurance, expired registration, and cell phone tickets.

Tickets from other agencies go elsewhere. Sheriff's deputies, DPS troopers and constables file in the Justice of the Peace courts, and Horizon City, Socorro and the smaller Lower Valley cities have their own municipal courts. The name of the issuing agency is printed near the top of your citation; if you can't tell, our free ticket and warrant lookup will find it for you.

Because Municipal Court handles only Class C misdemeanors — fine-only offenses with a maximum fine of $200 for most Transportation Code violations plus court costs — the court resolves the overwhelming majority of cases by negotiation on the pretrial docket rather than at trial.

sections.heading: How a Ticket Moves Through Municipal Court
paragraphs: Your citation lists an appearance date, usually 10 to 20 days after the stop. If nothing is filed by then, the court treats it as a failure to appear, adds a separate Class C charge under Transportation Code 543.009, and issues a warrant. When you hire us, we file a notice of appearance and a plea of not guilty on your behalf the same business day. That stops the clock and routes every notice to our office instead of your mailbox.

The case is then set on a pretrial docket. On that date Robert Navar or a member of our staff meets with the city prosecutor, reviews the officer's citation and notes, and negotiates. The prosecutor has standard offers for most charges, but the offer improves when the defense points out a defective citation, a missing element, or an officer who has left the department.

If the case can't be resolved by agreement, it is set for a bench or jury trial where the officer must appear and prove each element. Trials are rare for traffic tickets, and we would talk with you before taking that step.

sections.heading: What the Municipal Court Prosecutor and Judges Typically Offer
paragraphs: El Paso Municipal Court is generally receptive to deferred disposition under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051. The driver pays a special expense fee, stays violation-free for 90 to 180 days, and the case is dismissed with no conviction reported to DPS. For eligible drivers the court also allows a driving safety course dismissal under art. 45.0511 — a six-hour course, proof of completion and a driving record. Our deferred adjudication and defensive driving page covers who qualifies and who does not.

The court's habits are where local experience matters. Judges here are typically unwilling to offer defensive driving for speeds 25 mph or more over the limit, for CDL holders, or for drivers who used the course in the last 12 months. Those drivers need a lawyer to argue for deferral or a non-moving reduction. Compliance charges — no insurance, no driver's license, expired registration — are frequently dismissed outright when we show the prosecutor that the problem was fixed, which is why we ask for updated documents before the docket.

sections.heading: Our $59 Flat Fee for El Paso Municipal Court
paragraphs: We charge $59 per citation in El Paso Municipal Court — the lowest fee in our schedule, because Municipal Court is a few minutes from our office at 11860 Vista Del Sol Dr. and we are on its dockets every week. Each additional ticket from the same stop is a discounted add-on of $10 to $30 shown at checkout. The fee covers filing the appearance, the pretrial negotiation and the paperwork to close the case. Court fees for a deferral or course, if you choose that path, are paid to the court separately.

Compare that to what paying the ticket costs. Paying is a guilty plea; the conviction stays on your Texas record for three years, adds two points (three with a crash), and in most cases raises your insurance at every renewal. A $59 fee that keeps the conviction off the record is the cheaper option almost every time. The consultation is free, and se habla español.

sections.heading: Warrants and Holds From El Paso Municipal Court
paragraphs: Municipal Court issues warrants on missed appearance dates and missed payment deadlines, and the City of El Paso reports those cases to the state's Failure to Appear program under Transportation Code Chapter 706. That OMNI hold blocks your driver's license renewal at DPS until the court clears it.

We handle these every week. For $35 for the first warrant and $20 for each additional one, we file the appearance, ask the court to recall the warrant and reset the underlying ticket onto a docket, where it is then handled like any other case. Read more at traffic warrant recall and OMNI hold removal.

sections.heading: What to Do Before Your Municipal Court Date
paragraphs: Do not pay the ticket online, do not request defensive driving yourself (that request is treated as a plea), and do not let the appearance date pass. Find the citation number and the date, then hire us online or call 915-503-1600. Have your driver's license and current proof of insurance ready; if the ticket was for a compliance issue, fix it now so we can ask for a dismissal.
This page is general information, not legal advice about your case. We are glad to look at yours for free before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Where is El Paso Municipal Court?
faqs.a: El Paso Municipal Court is at 810 E. Overland Ave in downtown El Paso. It handles Class C citations written by the El Paso Police Department throughout the city. If you hire us, you generally do not need to go there at all — we appear for you.

faqs.q: How much does a lawyer cost for a ticket in El Paso Municipal Court?
faqs.a: Our flat fee is $59 per citation for El Paso Municipal Court. Additional tickets from the same stop are discounted add-ons, and the free consultation lets us confirm the fee before you pay anything.

faqs.q: Do I have to appear at 810 E. Overland if I hire you?
faqs.a: In most cases, no. We file an appearance, handle the pretrial docket and negotiate with the city prosecutor. You would only appear if the case were set for trial, which is uncommon and something we would discuss with you first.

faqs.q: My EPPD ticket is from months ago and I never went. What now?
faqs.a: There is likely a warrant and possibly an OMNI hold on your license. Call us the same day. We file an appearance, request the warrant recall and get the ticket back on a docket — see traffic warrant recall for the process and the $35 fee.

faqs.q: Will El Paso Municipal Court give me deferred disposition?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The court regularly grants deferred disposition under art. 45.051 for first-time or low-speed cases. Drivers cited at 25+ mph over, CDL holders and school-zone cases are harder, which is where having a lawyer request it makes the difference.

faqs.q: Can I check whether my ticket is in Municipal Court or another court?
faqs.a: Yes. Use our free ticket and warrant lookup and we will tell you which court has the case, whether a warrant exists and what the fee would be.
